newsitem.title: USA: Swiss and Jews pledge cooperation over kosher lunch.
newsitem.headline: Swiss and Jews pledge cooperation over kosher lunch.

text.p: Switzerland's foreign minister and the president of the Jewish group that led the effort to expose wartime Swiss economic links with the Nazis sat down to a kosher lunch on Thursday and agreed their confrontation was over.

Heads of major Swiss banks and businesses and major U.S. Jewish organisations also attended the lunch held by World Jewish Congress President Edgar Bronfman in honour of Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti.

Both men said afterwards that the lunch at the Four Seasons Restaurant, which had to call a special caterer in to serve a kosher meal, had major symbolic signifigance. Cotti also used the occasion to apologise for Switzerland's turning back of 30,000 Jews seeking refuge from the Nazis during the war.

"Today's meeting signals a 180-degree change. ... It is important for the rest of Europe to take note that Switzerland is now willing to face its past so it can have an honourable future," Bronfman said.

He was referring to Swiss plans to set up funds to benefit Holocaust survivors and other victims of repression and to form a historian's commission to evaluate Swiss dealings with the Nazis during the war.
Just three months ago the outgoing Swiss president had accused Jewish groups of blackmail and extortion for calling for a goodwill financial gesture on Switzerland's part.

Bronfman called on Poland, the Czech Republic, Spain, Portugal, Holland, Belgium, Sweden and France to follow suit, saying in a speech to the group, "All European countries must now look back, just as Switzerland is looking back, squarely facing a period of shame. ... France must fairly address its Vichy government and its egregious past."

Cotti said the lunch put a symbolic stamp on the fact that his country, after initial anger and hostility, had moved from confrontation to cooperation with Jewish groups and was anxious to fairly face its past.

In an emotional address to the group, he noted that international media had seized on the revelations about Switzerland to "derive a certain pleasure from exposing the dark side of the history of a small country long considered to be the poster boy of propriety within the international community."
But he added there was no doubt that there were dark moments in Swiss history during the 1930s and 40s.

"This is a fact we must accept without any ifs and buts," he said, adding that he apologised for such Swiss actions as turning away 30,000 Jews at the Swiss border and inventing the Jewish "J" stamp to be put on German passports.

Both Bronfman and Cotti said they expected that money from the almost $300 million fund organised to aid Holocaust survivors would begin being distributed in the next few weeks or months and they said a board to administer the fund would be announced next week.

Meanwhile, New York Republican Senator Alfonse D'Amato, a major U.S. critic of the Swiss, said the Swiss National Bank had confirmed in a letter a charge made in U.S. intelligence documents that Switzerland shipped 126 truckloads of German gold to Spain. The gold was worth about $200 million at the time.
